query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: For high-entropy alloys, a combined approach using high-throughput, standardized calorimetric and densitometric measurements integrated with first-principles‐calibrated molecular dynamics simulations can accurately extract melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume changes at melting, and key liquid-phase thermodynamic properties.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast or homogenized NiFeCoCr-based high-entropy alloys (and derivatives with controlled FCC metal additions such as Pd) in a single-phase disordered state.
generation.intervention: Implementing a protocol that first characterizes the alloy using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and high-pressure densitometry under controlled atmospheres and heating rates, and then calibrating molecular dynamics simulation models using ab initio data, to establish a reproducible mapping between atomic-level disorder and macroscopic thermodynamic transitions.
generation.conditions: Measurements are performed under inert atmospheres, with controlled heating and cooling rates to minimize kinetic effects, in alloys that maintain chemical homogeneity (i.e. avoiding phase-separation or decomposition).
generation.structural_mediator: The local atomic configurations and distribution of coordination environments (which govern configurational and vibrational entropic contributions) mediate the relationship between composition and the thermodynamic properties at melting.
generation.mechanism: The intervention leverages precise experimental measurements to capture enthalpic and volumetric changes during melting while simulation models refine the interpretation by accounting for distributed energy landscapes inherent in high-entropy alloys. This joint experimental–computational framework reduces systematic errors common in standalone measurements and simulations by directly correlating microstructural disorder with macroscopic thermodynamic behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: The integrated approach will yield melting temperatures, enthalpy/entropy of fusion, and volume change values with an expected quantitative performance improvement, reducing the relative error in predictions to below approximately 5–10% compared to conventional DSC or simulation-only methods over a wide range of compositions within the high-entropy-alloy family.
generation.baseline: Traditional standalone calorimetric (e.g., DSC) or simulation methods typically exhibit relative errors of 10–20% and often lack the resolution to decouple configurational contributions from intrinsic phase transformation energetics.
generation.boundary: This approach is anticipated to be robust for chemically homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloys. Its applicability may be limited for systems undergoing significant phase segregation, decomposition, or where kinetic delays obscure equilibrium thermodynamic signals.
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain whether the simulation calibration can universally capture all complex local fluctuations in heavily disordered systems, especially for alloys near multiphase boundaries. Further, the sensitivity of high-throughput experimental setups to subtle volume changes at melting may introduce additional uncertainties.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a representative set of NiFeCoCr-based high-entropy alloys (including with Pd additions) that are known to exhibit single-phase behavior. For each alloy, first measure the melting temperature, enthalpy/entropy of fusion and volume change with high-resolution DSC and densitometry data under controlled conditions. Independently, run ab initio-calibrated molecular dynamics simulations to predict the same properties under identical conditions. Compare the predicted and measured values for each alloy.
measurements: DSC for heat flow and transition temperature
High-pressure densitometry for volume change at melting
Calorimetric determination of fusion enthalpy and derived entropy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the integrated approach yields predictions that differ consistently by more than 10% from the experimental measurements for over 70% of the tested high-entropy alloys, or if the simulation fails to capture key trends observed in the experiments (e.g., systematic under- or over-estimation of the fusion properties), then the hypothesis—that this combined methodology can accurately and efficiently determine the target thermodynamic properties—will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Tunable magnetocaloric effect in transition metal alloys

Abstract: The unpredictability of geopolitical tensions and resulting supply chain and pricing instabilities make it imperative to explore rare earth free magnetic materials. As such, we have investigated fully transition metal based “high entropy alloys” in the context of the magnetocaloric effect. We find the NiFeCoCrPdx family exhibits a second order magnetic phase transition whose critical temperature is tunable from 100 K to well above room temperature. The system notably displays changes in the functionality of the magnetic entropy change depending on x, which leads to nearly 40% enhancement of the refrigerant capacity. A detailed statistical analysis of the universal scaling behavior provides direct evidence that heat treatment and Pd additions reduce the distribution of exchange energies in the system, leading to a more magnetically homogeneous alloy. The general implications of this work are that the parent NiFeCoCr compound can be tuned dramatically with FCC metal additives.
